claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the predation assays.

claims.claim: Predation of both larvae and eggs without GLV supplementation was two to four times as great on GLV-emitting WT and irPI plants during M3.
claims.source: Predation of both larvae and eggs without GLV supplementation was two to four times as great on GLV-emitting WT and irPI plants: 43%/60% (WT/irPI) for larvae and 34%/39% for eggs, vs 17%/33% (irLOX2/hemi-irLOX2) for larvae and 9%/20% for eggs (Fisher's exact tests: N=30 larvae, p=0.047 for irLOX2 vs WT, p=0.069 for hemi-irLOX2 vs irPI; N=88 eggs, p<0.001 for irLOX2 vs WT, p=0.013 for hemi-irLOX2 vs irPI) (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the predation assays.

claims.claim: There was no difference among plant genotypes in the number of Geocoris spp. individuals during M3.
claims.source: However, there was no difference among plant genotypes in the number of Geocoris spp. individuals (p>0.05 in Fisher's exact tests), indicating that Geocoris spp. regularly survey all plants and use GLVs as a short-distance cue to determine which plants harbor prey.
claims.evidence: This is a result from Geocoris spp. counts.

claims.claim: Geocoris spp. regularly survey all plants and use GLVs as a short-distance cue to determine which plants harbor prey.
claims.source: However, there was no difference among plant genotypes in the number of Geocoris spp. individuals (p>0.05 in Fisher's exact tests), indicating that Geocoris spp. regularly survey all plants and use GLVs as a short-distance cue to determine which plants harbor prey.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the Geocoris spp. count data.

claims.claim: Over the following week after the beginning of M3, Geocoris spp. predated a total of 80% of larvae from WT and irPI vs 47% from irLOX2 and 67% from hemi-irLOX2.
claims.source: Figure 5 shows larval predation rates at the beginning of the assay, when the M. sexta load was comparable across plant genotypes. Over the following week, Geocoris spp. predated a total of 80% of these larvae from WT and irPI vs 47% from irLOX2 (Fisher's exact test, p=0.015 vs WT) and 67% from hemi-irLOX2 (p=0.382 vs irPI).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from extended predation monitoring.

claims.claim: Geocoris spp. had the same opportunity to locate M. sexta larvae and eggs on all genotypes, but consistently preferred to predate from GLV-supplemented or -emitting plants.
claims.source: In summary, Geocoris spp. had the same opportunity to locate M. sexta larvae and eggs on all genotypes, but consistently preferred to predate from GLV-supplemented or -emitting plants.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the predation experiments.

claims.claim: The irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants suffered a similar amount of M. sexta damage to WT plants in trials M2 and M3.
claims.source: The irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants suffered, in total, a similar amount of M. sexta damage to WT plants in trials M2 and M3 (Figure 4), and only irPI plants suffered significantly less M. sexta damage (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a result from damage assessments.

claims.claim: Only irPI plants suffered significantly less M. sexta damage in trials M2 and M3.
claims.source: The irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants suffered, in total, a similar amount of M. sexta damage to WT plants in trials M2 and M3 (Figure 4), and only irPI plants suffered significantly less M. sexta damage (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a result from damage assessments.

claims.claim: Reduced predation of M. sexta from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 in trials M2 and M3 in 2011 correlated with the reduced growth and reproduction of both genotypes.
claims.source: Reduced predation of M. sexta from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 in trials M2 and M3 in 2011 (Figure 4) correlated with the reduced growth and reproduction of both genotypes, by 30–50% for irLOX2 and 20–30% for hemi-irLOX2 vs WT, although this reduction was also apparent in plants not infested with M. sexta. (Figures 4 and 6, statistics Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is a correlation observed in the data.

claims.claim: The reduction in growth and reproduction of irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 was also apparent in plants not infested with M. sexta in 2011.
claims.source: Reduced predation of M. sexta from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 in trials M2 and M3 in 2011 (Figure 4) correlated with the reduced growth and reproduction of both genotypes, by 30–50% for irLOX2 and 20–30% for hemi-irLOX2 vs WT, although this reduction was also apparent in plants not infested with M. sexta. (Figures 4 and 6, statistics Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is an observation that complicates the interpretation of the 2011 data.

claims.claim: In 2010, in the absence of predation, there was no difference in stem growth, branching, or bud and flower production among genotypes irrespective of M. sexta infestation.
claims.source: In 2010 however, in the absence of predation, there was no difference in stem growth, branching, or bud and flower production among genotypes irrespective of M. sexta infestation (Figure 6, statistics Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the 2010 field experiment.

claims.claim: M. sexta feeding significantly affected growth and reproduction of plants overall in 2011.
claims.source: Although M. sexta feeding significantly affected growth and reproduction of plants overall, the effect was not significant for irLOX2 or irPI plants in either year (Figure 6, statistics Table 3), possibly due to reduced feeding damage resulting from a lack of TPI-induced compensatory feeding in irPI (Steppuhn and Baldwin, 2007) (Mann-Whitney U-test between irPI and WT on May 28, U=54, p=0.046, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the growth and reproduction data.

claims.claim: The effect of M. sexta feeding on growth and reproduction was not significant for irLOX2 or irPI plants in either year.
claims.source: Although M. sexta feeding significantly affected growth and reproduction of plants overall, the effect was not significant for irLOX2 or irPI plants in either year (Figure 6, statistics Table 3), possibly due to reduced feeding damage resulting from a lack of TPI-induced compensatory feeding in irPI (Steppuhn and Baldwin, 2007) (Mann-Whitney U-test between irPI and WT on May 28, U=54, p=0.046, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the growth and reproduction data.

claims.claim: The lack of significant M. sexta feeding effect on irPI plants may be due to reduced feeding damage resulting from a lack of TPI-induced compensatory feeding.
claims.source: Although M. sexta feeding significantly affected growth and reproduction of plants overall, the effect was not significant for irLOX2 or irPI plants in either year (Figure 6, statistics Table 3), possibly due to reduced feeding damage resulting from a lack of TPI-induced compensatory feeding in irPI (Steppuhn and Baldwin, 2007) (Mann-Whitney U-test between irPI and WT on May 28, U=54, p=0.046, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on previous findings and current data.

claims.claim: M. sexta feeding reduced flower production rates by about 50% in WT and by about 30% in hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2010.
claims.source: Yet hemi-irLOX2 plants, despite strongly reduced GLVs, still suffered reduced growth and reproduction from Manduca spp. feeding: M. sexta feeding reduced flower production rates by about 50% in WT and by about 30% in hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2010, although the overall reduction was only significant in WT; and reduced bud production significantly for both WT and hemi-irLOX2 by 25–30% in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the 2010 experiment.

claims.claim: M. sexta feeding reduced bud production significantly for both WT and hemi-irLOX2 by 25–30% in 2011.
claims.source: Yet hemi-irLOX2 plants, despite strongly reduced GLVs, still suffered reduced growth and reproduction from Manduca spp. feeding: M. sexta feeding reduced flower production rates by about 50% in WT and by about 30% in hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2010, although the overall reduction was only significant in WT; and reduced bud production significantly for both WT and hemi-irLOX2 by 25–30% in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the 2011 experiment.

claims.claim: All genotypes were attacked by mirid (Tupiocoris notatus) and noctuid herbivores which caused similar amounts of damage across genotypes and years.
claims.source: All genotypes were attacked by mirid (Tupiocoris notatus) and noctuid herbivores which caused similar amounts of damage across genotypes and years (ca. 15% and 3% of total canopy area, respectively) although irLOX2 plants suffered 60% less mirid and noctuid damage by the end of M3 in 2011 (N=24–28; Bonferroni-corrected Kruskal-Wallis test, noctuids May 5, p=0.027, all pairwise tests Bonferroni-corrected p>0.05; one-way ANOVAs with factor genotype on arcsine-transformed data: mirids May 27, F3,103=5.291, p=0.002, p<0.05 for irLOX2 vs hemi-irLOX2 and irPI in Scheffe post hoc tests, noctuids May 27, F3,103=3.503, p=0.018, all post hoc tests p>0.05; all other comparisons p>0.05; Figures 4 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is a result from herbivore damage monitoring.

claims.claim: irLOX2 plants suffered 60% less mirid and noctuid damage by the end of M3 in 2011.
claims.source: All genotypes were attacked by mirid (Tupiocoris notatus) and noctuid herbivores which caused similar amounts of damage across genotypes and years (ca. 15% and 3% of total canopy area, respectively) although irLOX2 plants suffered 60% less mirid and noctuid damage by the end of M3 in 2011 (N=24–28; Bonferroni-corrected Kruskal-Wallis test, noctuids May 5, p=0.027, all pairwise tests Bonferroni-corrected p>0.05; one-way ANOVAs with factor genotype on arcsine-transformed data: mirids May 27, F3,103=5.291, p=0.002, p<0.05 for irLOX2 vs hemi-irLOX2 and irPI in Scheffe post hoc tests, noctuids May 27, F3,103=3.503, p=0.018, all post hoc tests p>0.05; all other comparisons p>0.05; Figures 4 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from herbivore damage monitoring.

claims.claim: Reduced herbivore damage on irLOX2 in 2011 could have increased the growth and reproduction of irLOX2 plants relative to WT, but cannot explain why irLOX2 plants instead displayed reduced growth and reproduction.
claims.source: Reduced herbivore damage on irLOX2 in 2011 could have increased the growth and reproduction of irLOX2 plants relative to WT, but cannot explain why irLOX2 plants instead displayed reduced growth and reproduction.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the damage and fitness data.

claims.claim: Plants in 2011 were also damaged by flea beetles and grasshoppers (<3% of canopy area).
claims.source: Plants in 2011 were also damaged by flea beetles and grasshoppers (<3% of canopy area, Kruskal-Wallis tests, N=24–28, all comparisons p>0.05, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a result from herbivore damage monitoring.

claims.claim: Reduced growth and reproduction of uninfested irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2011 might have been due to non-herbivory-related factors.
claims.source: We cannot exclude the possibility that reduced growth and reproduction of uninfested irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) might have been due to non-herbivory-related factors (e.g., differences in root health corresponding to GLV antimicrobial properties) which did not play a role in 2010.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations.

claims.claim: Assay M4 is the more robust basis for the argument that GLV-mediated indirect defense increases plant reproduction.
claims.source: Because of this uncertainty, we conducted assay M4 (Figure 4) in which plants were carefully matched for size and prior reproduction (Figure 8), and this experiment is the more robust basis for our argument that GLV-mediated indirect defense increases plant reproduction.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological justification by the authors.

claims.claim: In both 2010 and 2011, triplets of WT, irPI and hemi-irLOX2 plants were selected that were similar in size, reproductive output, apparent health, and prior damage.
claims.source: In both 2010 and 2011, we selected triplets of WT, irPI and hemi-irLOX2 plants similar in size, reproductive output, apparent health, and prior damage; damage from naturally occurring herbivores did not differ among these genotypes (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for M1 and M4.

claims.claim: In the absence of Geocoris spp. in 2010, genotypes did not differ in M. sexta mortality or plant reproduction.
claims.source: In the absence of Geocoris spp. in 2010, genotypes did not differ in M. sexta mortality (N=51 larvae)—which in every observed case was due to a failure of the larva to feed—or plant reproduction (N=17 plants) (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the 2010 M1 experiment.

claims.claim: M. sexta mortality in 2010 was in every observed case due to a failure of the larva to feed.
claims.source: In the absence of Geocoris spp. in 2010, genotypes did not differ in M. sexta mortality (N=51 larvae)—which in every observed case was due to a failure of the larva to feed—or plant reproduction (N=17 plants) (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the cause of mortality in 2010.

claims.claim: Flower removal itself does not cause a difference among genotypes.
claims.source: This, and the fact that flower production did not differ among genotypes in 2011 through infestation M3 despite flower removal (Figure 6), indicates that flower removal itself does not cause a difference among genotypes, and suggests that the other differences among genotypes in growth and reproduction seen in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) are real.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the flower removal control.

claims.claim: The differences among genotypes in growth and reproduction seen in 2011 are real.
claims.source: This, and the fact that flower production did not differ among genotypes in 2011 through infestation M3 despite flower removal (Figure 6), indicates that flower removal itself does not cause a difference among genotypes, and suggests that the other differences among genotypes in growth and reproduction seen in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) are real.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the control experiments.

claims.claim: In 2011, all reproductive meristems were removed from matched plants by cutting inflorescences at their base prior to M4.
claims.source: In 2011, hemi-irLOX2, irPI and WT plants were matched prior to infestation M4 to exclude differences in growth, reproduction and Manduca spp. damage arising during M. sexta infestations M2 and M3 and from caged Manduca spp. during the egg predation assay (Figures 4, 7, and 8). Instead of regularly removing flowers, we removed all reproductive meristems from matched plants in 2011 by cutting inflorescences at their base.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for M4.

claims.claim: Removing reproductive meristems allowed following a new set of reproductive meristems through to seed set without incurring ripe seed.
claims.source: This allowed us to follow a new set of reproductive meristems through to seed set without incurring ripe seed.
claims.evidence: This is a justification for the meristem removal procedure.

claims.claim: A similar number of reproductive meristems were cut from all plants in M4, and thus all plants were similarly affected by this cutting.
claims.source: Because plants were matched prior to the assay, a similar number of reproductive meristems were cut from all plants, and thus all plants were similarly affected by this cutting (Figure 8, see 'Discussion').
claims.evidence: This is a justification that the meristem removal did not bias the results.

claims.claim: Oviposition by native Manduca spp. moths provided sufficient eggs prior to the beginning of M4.
claims.source: Because oviposition by native Manduca spp. moths provided sufficient eggs prior to the beginning of M4 (Figure 4), we decided to conduct this infestation with wild larvae and thereby demonstrate that native larvae, like larvae of the lab strain, are susceptible to GLV-mediated predation.
claims.evidence: This is an observation that allowed use of wild larvae.

claims.claim: Native Manduca spp. larvae, like larvae of the lab strain, are susceptible to GLV-mediated predation.
claims.source: Because oviposition by native Manduca spp. moths provided sufficient eggs prior to the beginning of M4 (Figure 4), we decided to conduct this infestation with wild larvae and thereby demonstrate that native larvae, like larvae of the lab strain, are susceptible to GLV-mediated predation.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in M4.

claims.claim: One wild Manduca spp. neonate per plant was placed on a lower stem leaf to mimic natural oviposition rates in M4.
claims.source: To make M4 a realistic test, we placed one wild Manduca spp. neonate per plant on a lower stem leaf to mimic natural oviposition rates (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for M4.

claims.claim: During the first to third larval instars, wild Manduca spp. mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 plants vs 62–76% on matched WT and irPI plants in M4.
claims.source: During the first to third larval instars in which larvae are vulnerable to Geocoris spp. predation (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001), wild Manduca spp. mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 plants vs 62–76% on matched WT and irPI plants; the overall mortality of larvae on all three lines was significantly different (N=21 larvae, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons by Friedman tests, p<0.01) (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the M4 experiment.

claims.claim: The overall mortality of wild Manduca spp. larvae on all three lines was significantly different in M4.
claims.source: During the first to third larval instars in which larvae are vulnerable to Geocoris spp. predation (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001), wild Manduca spp. mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 plants vs 62–76% on matched WT and irPI plants; the overall mortality of larvae on all three lines was significantly different (N=21 larvae, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons by Friedman tests, p<0.01) (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the M4 experiment.

claims.claim: Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar.
claims.source: Although Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar, this was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards (Cnemidophorus spp.) which were present on the field plot: these lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes (Stork et al., 2011; Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the M4 experiment.

claims.claim: The increased mortality on hemi-irLOX2 in the fourth instar was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards.
claims.source: Although Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar, this was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards (Cnemidophorus spp.) which were present on the field plot: these lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes (Stork et al., 2011; Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observations and cited literature.

claims.claim: Whiptail lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes.
claims.source: Although Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar, this was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards (Cnemidophorus spp.) which were present on the field plot: these lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes (Stork et al., 2011; Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is information from cited literature.

claims.claim: The hemi-irLOX2 plants had produced 40–50% fewer buds and flowers than matched WT and irPI plants by the end of M4.
claims.source: By the end of the assay, the hemi-irLOX2 plants had produced 40–50% fewer buds and flowers than matched WT and irPI plants (N=21 plants, p<0.05 in Scheffe post hoc tests for hemi-irLOX2 vs WT and irPI flowers and buds following a repeated-measures MANOVA over all flower and bud counts, Wilks' Lambda for the interaction of line and day: F12,110=2.835, p=0.002) (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the M4 experiment.

claims.claim: The reduced bud and flower production in hemi-irLOX2 was not due to accelerated seed set.
claims.source: This reduced bud and flower production was not due to accelerated seed set: unripe seed capsules on hemi-irLOX2 plants were also reduced by 50% (N=21 plants, p=0.021 for hemi-irLOX2 vs irPI in a Scheffe post hoc test following an ANOVA with genotype as the factor, F2,60=4.142, p=0.021) (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: This is a result ruling out an alternative explanation.

claims.claim: Herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. larvae twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. larvae twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the M4 experiment.

claims.claim: M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata did not differ in their growth or instar progression on plants in M4.
claims.source: M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata did not differ in their growth or instar progression (N=11–13, repeated measures ANOVA for days 4–11, Wilks' Lambda for the interaction of day and species: F11,12=1.356, p=0.311).
claims.evidence: This is a result from analysis of the two Manduca species.

claims.claim: It is likely that mortality of M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata was equal prior to the third instar in M4.
claims.source: Because larvae of the two species cannot be distinguished before the third instar, we could not test whether mortality was equal for both species in the first three instars; however, because other collections of wild eggs around the same time as the collection for our experiment yielded a 1:1 ratio of species, and because our ratio of the species remained 1:1 after larvae reached the third instar, it is likely that mortality of the two species was equal prior to the third instar.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on species ratios.

claims.claim: TPIs had a less consistent and negative effect on Manduca spp. predation.
claims.source: TPIs had a less consistent and, contrary to our expectations, negative effect on Manduca spp. predation (Figure 5); furthermore, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) and only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions (N=13–26 second instar larvae during M2, one-way ANOVAs with genotype as the factor, F3,77=2.792, p=0.046, all post hoc tests p>0.05, Figure 10; N=8 second instar larvae during M4, paired t-test between matched WT and irPI, p=0.052).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of results regarding TPIs.

claims.claim: There was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction.
claims.source: TPIs had a less consistent and, contrary to our expectations, negative effect on Manduca spp. predation (Figure 5); furthermore, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) and only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions (N=13–26 second instar larvae during M2, one-way ANOVAs with genotype as the factor, F3,77=2.792, p=0.046, all post hoc tests p>0.05, Figure 10; N=8 second instar larvae during M4, paired t-test between matched WT and irPI, p=0.052).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the fitness measurements.

claims.claim: There was only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions.
claims.source: TPIs had a less consistent and, contrary to our expectations, negative effect on Manduca spp. predation (Figure 5); furthermore, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) and only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions (N=13–26 second instar larvae during M2, one-way ANOVAs with genotype as the factor, F3,77=2.792, p=0.046, all post hoc tests p>0.05, Figure 10; N=8 second instar larvae during M4, paired t-test between matched WT and irPI, p=0.052).
claims.evidence: This is a result from larval growth measurements.

claims.claim: Wild Manduca spp. larvae feeding on WT plants reacted more sluggishly to experimental provocation than size-matched larvae on irPI plants.
claims.source: Indeed, wild Manduca spp. larvae feeding on WT plants (infestation M4, Figure 4) reacted more sluggishly to experimental provocation than size-matched larvae on irPI plants: they were 75% less likely to attack when lifted off of the leaf (N=5 second-instar larvae matched for size, p=0.035 in paired t-test) (Figure 10, Videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the on-plant behavioral assay.

claims.claim: Wild Manduca spp. larvae on WT plants were 75% less likely to attack when lifted off of the leaf compared to larvae on irPI plants.
claims.source: Indeed, wild Manduca spp. larvae feeding on WT plants (infestation M4, Figure 4) reacted more sluggishly to experimental provocation than size-matched larvae on irPI plants: they were 75% less likely to attack when lifted off of the leaf (N=5 second-instar larvae matched for size, p=0.035 in paired t-test) (Figure 10, Videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral assay.

claims.claim: Larvae fed on WT leaves were 50% less likely to successfully attack the insect pin in the off-plant assay.
claims.source: Similarly to the on-plant assay, larvae fed on WT leaves were 50% less likely to successfully attack the insect pin, either when initially poked, or poked and lifted with the pin (N=20 first-instar larvae matched for size, p<0.05 in paired t-tests) (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the off-plant behavioral assay.

claims.claim: WT-fed larvae ceased to grow for at least 24 hr after simulated attack, while irPI-fed larvae continued to grow.
claims.source: We also monitored recovery post-trial and found that WT-fed larvae ceased to grow for at least 24 hr after simulated attack, while irPI-fed larvae continued to grow (p=0.016 in Student's t-test); mortality did not differ (p=0.527 in Fisher's exact test) (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the recovery monitoring after the behavioral assay.

claims.claim: Mortality did not differ between WT-fed and irPI-fed larvae after simulated attack.
claims.source: We also monitored recovery post-trial and found that WT-fed larvae ceased to grow for at least 24 hr after simulated attack, while irPI-fed larvae continued to grow (p=0.016 in Student's t-test); mortality did not differ (p=0.527 in Fisher's exact test) (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the recovery monitoring.

claims.claim: TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
claims.source: Thus TPIs did not increase plant reproduction under attack from Manduca spp. in nature, but may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral assays.

claims.claim: The contradictory higher predation rates of Manduca spp. larvae from irPI than from WT plants might reflect Geocoris spp.'s feeding preference if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae.
claims.source: The contradictory higher predation rates of Manduca spp. larvae from irPI than from WT plants (Figure 5) might reflect Geocoris spp.'s feeding preference, if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae (Kaplan and Thaler, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation to explain an unexpected result.

claims.claim: Herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
claims.source: Our data demonstrate that herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: There was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction and no significant effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction and no significant effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions; however, TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of TPI results stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
claims.source: In contrast, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction and no significant effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions; however, TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral data stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The tendency towards higher predation rates from irPI than from WT plants could reflect Geocoris spp.'s preference if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae.
claims.source: Although this indicates that predation rates from irPI plants should be reduced, we observed a tendency towards higher predation rates from irPI than from WT plants; this could reflect Geocoris spp.'s preference if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae (Kaplan and Thaler, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation to explain an unexpected result stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Functional RNAi constructs may be rendered ineffective as a result of insufficient gene dosage when present in the hemizygous state.
claims.source: It is common molecular biology knowledge that functional RNAi constructs may be rendered ineffective as a result of insufficient gene dosage, for example, Travella et al. results.result: The transgenic lines irPI and irLOX2 successfully silenced their target genes (TPI and GLV production respectively) without affecting non-target defense metabolites. irPI plants showed no detectable TPI activity and 0.3% PI transcript levels. irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants showed 80-100% reduction in GLV emissions, with LOX2 transcripts at 2% of WT. Importantly, (E)-α-bergamotene emission was unaffected in all lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C85 provide comprehensive molecular and chemical characterization of the transgenic lines. Multiple independent measurements (TPI activity, transcript levels, GLV pools, headspace emissions) consistently demonstrate successful gene silencing with appropriate specificity. Statistical tests support significant differences. The characterization includes both field and glasshouse conditions, strengthening confidence in the phenotypes.

results.result: The irPI construct was unexpectedly inactive in hemizygous irLOX2 plants created by crossing homozygous irLOX2 and irPI lines. This is attributed to gene dosage effects or promoter methylation affecting RNAi construct expression in the hemizygous state.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 document the observation, while C149-C150 provide mechanistic explanations supported by citations. The data in C73-C75 confirm that hemi-irLOX2 plants have WT-level TPI activity. This is a well-documented phenomenon in molecular biology, and the authors appropriately acknowledge and explain this unexpected result.

results.result: Geocoris spp. predators consistently preferred to predate Manduca larvae and eggs from GLV-emitting or GLV-supplemented plants. In 2010, no Geocoris were present. In 2011, predation was 2-4 times higher on WT/irPI plants (43-60% larvae, 34-39% eggs) compared to irLOX2/hemi-irLOX2 plants (17-33% larvae, 9-20% eggs). Geocoris populations did not differ among genotypes, indicating they survey all plants but use GLVs as short-distance cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C97 present a coherent story of predation patterns across two years. The 2010 control (no predators) is crucial for interpretation. Statistical tests (Fisher's exact tests) support differences in predation rates. The experimental design with GLV supplementation in M2 (C89-C92) followed by removal in M3 (C93-C96) provides strong evidence for GLV-mediated predation. Geocoris counts (C94) rule out differential attraction to plant genotypes.

results.result: In 2011, reduced Geocoris predation on irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants correlated with 30-50% and 20-30% reductions in growth and reproduction respectively. However, this reduction was also apparent in uninfested plants, complicating interpretation. In 2010, without Geocoris predation, no fitness differences were observed among genotypes. M. sexta feeding significantly affected plant fitness overall, but effects varied by genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C112 reveal a critical confound in the 2011 data: fitness differences appear even without herbivory (C101, C112). While C102 shows no differences in 2010, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether non-herbivory factors affected 2011 results. This undermines confidence in attributing 2011 fitness differences solely to differential predation. The authors appropriately conduct M4 to address this (C113).

results.result: In carefully matched plant triplets (M4, 2011), wild Manduca mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 vs 62-76% on WT/irPI during vulnerable instars (significantly different, p<0.01). This resulted in hemi-irLOX2 plants producing 40-50% fewer buds and flowers than matched WT/irPI plants. In 2010 without Geocoris, no differences in mortality or reproduction were observed. This demonstrates that GLV-mediated predation increases plant fitness twofold.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C132 present the most robust test of the main hypothesis. The matching procedure (C114, C119-C121) controls for confounds identified in earlier experiments. Using wild Manduca larvae (C122-C124) increases ecological relevance. Statistical tests support significant differences in both mortality (C126) and reproduction (C130-C131). The 2010 control (C115-C116) is essential for ruling out direct effects of GLV silencing. This is the strongest evidence for the fitness benefit of GLVs.

results.result: M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata did not differ in growth or instar progression on plants, and mortality was likely equal for both species based on 1:1 ratios before and after the third instar.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 address a potential confound from using mixed wild Manduca species. The statistical test (repeated measures ANOVA, p=0.311) and inference from species ratios support equal performance. This validates pooling the two species in mortality analyses.

results.result: TPIs did not increase plant fitness and had only marginal effects on Manduca growth under field conditions. However, larvae feeding on TPI-producing plants showed 75% reduced attack responses when provoked on plants and 50% reduced attack success in off-plant assays. WT-fed larvae also ceased growth for 24 hr after simulated attack while irPI-fed larvae continued growing. This suggests TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening herbivore escape responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C143 present consistent evidence across multiple behavioral assays (on-plant and off-plant) with appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, p<0.05). The lack of fitness benefit (C136) contrasts with the behavioral effects, leading to the reasonable inference that TPIs enhance indirect defense (C143). However, C144 notes a contradictory finding of higher predation on irPI plants, which the authors speculatively attribute to larval nutritional quality.

results.result: The main conclusion is that herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing Manduca predation twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat, but only when Geocoris predators are present to reduce herbivore loads by 50%.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C132, and C145 state the main conclusion, which is supported by the M4 experiment results. The conditional nature (requiring Geocoris presence) is crucial and well-demonstrated by comparing 2010 (no predators, no fitness benefit) with 2011 (predators present, fitness benefit). The twofold increase is quantitatively supported by data in C125-C126 (mortality) and C130 (reproduction).

results.result: Bud and flower production is justified as a proxy for Darwinian fitness in N. attenuata because: (1) it's an annual with seeds produced in one season mostly via self-pollination (>70%), (2) <5% of buds/flowers are aborted by healthy plants, (3) bud/flower numbers correlate with seed production, and (4) transgenic lines don't differ in seed mass or viability. The meristem removal procedure in M4 affected all matched plants similarly.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 and C151-C154 provide strong justification for the fitness proxy, supported by citations and field observations. Claims C155-C157 address a potential confound in M4, showing that despite hemi-irLOX2 having more prior flowers, the number of inflorescences cut was similar across genotypes. This methodological transparency strengthens confidence in the M4 results.

results.result: The introduction establishes that while HIPVs are known to attract predators and reduce herbivore loads by 24-90%, it has remained unclear for three decades whether HIPVs increase plant fitness because they can be intercepted by other organisms. Previous studies were too short-term or didn't measure fitness. Long-term field studies with endogenously produced, inducible HIPVs are required to demonstrate defensive function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C32 accurately summarize the state of knowledge and identify the key gap motivating the study. The citations support the claims about HIPV functions and the limitations of previous work. The methodological requirements (C24-C32) are well-justified and directly inform the experimental design.

results.result: The introduction establishes the biological context for TPIs: they slow Manduca growth on N. attenuata by reducing protein digestion, but herbivores can overcome them by various mechanisms including eating more tissue (which could reduce plant fitness). While TPI-producing plants had higher seed production than TPI-deficient plants in glasshouse conditions, whether TPIs function as defenses in nature was unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C43 provide appropriate background on TPIs supported by citations. The logic connecting TPI effects to the slow-growth-high-mortality hypothesis (C34) is sound. The acknowledgment that some herbivore counter-adaptations could reduce plant fitness (C41) shows balanced consideration of alternatives.

results.result: The study system is well-characterized: Manduca spp. are major herbivores of N. attenuata in Utah, and Geocoris spp. predators naturally occur there and are attracted to GLVs and (E)-α-bergamotene. GLVs can be silenced via NaLOX2, are released immediately upon damage, and have multiple ecological functions including attracting both predators and herbivores, priming neighboring plants, and serving as cues for pollinators. GLVs also stimulate Manduca feeding.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C66 establish the ecological and molecular context, all supported by appropriate citations. The multifunctional nature of GLVs (C61-C64) is important for understanding why fitness effects might be complex. The fact that GLVs stimulate herbivore feeding (C65-C66) is a critical consideration that could work against any defensive benefit.

results.result: The authors conclude that demonstrating HIPV defensive function sets the stage for using HIPVs in integrated pest management (IPM). They recommend selective breeding or engineering of HIPV emission rather than controlled release dispensers. PIs could enhance indirect defense efficiency, especially combined with Bt toxins. With growing Bt resistance concerns, indirect defenses promise an effective first line of defense to which herbivores are unlikely to rapidly evolve resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C167 present reasonable applications and implications, but they extend beyond what the data directly support. The study demonstrates fitness benefits in one native plant-herbivore-predator system, but extrapolation to agricultural IPM (C158-C163) requires additional validation. The claim about resistance evolution (C167) is speculative, though plausible. These are appropriate discussion points but should be tested empirically.
